title: Sheelogheyn
description: Ten short stories about generations: a stonemason and his grandson cut a granite slab, a girl spends a spring week on her grandmother's farm, a letter from an aunt in Japan, a grandmother's old tale of a tournament, a linguist grandmother helps with a school project on grammar, a grandfather and granddaughter at the microscope, an old man who forgets but still plays the blues, a great-grandmother who flew aeroplanes, a socialist grandfather's box of old papers, and the family mill by the river.

lessons.title: Y masoonagh as e vac-y-vac
lessons.summary: Algernon Teare, eighty, was a stonemason in Peel for fifty years and is now stooped; his grandson Tristram, sixteen, wants to learn the trade, which was always Algernon's hope: together they measure a granite slab with a yard rod for the grave of Tristram's great-grandmother, cut her name and the date, and add her name in ogham as on the old stones; Algernon teaches that a mason needs courtesy with families who have lost someone.
lessons.text:
Ta Algernon Teare kiare feed bleeaney d'eash. Va eh ny masoonagh ayns Purt ny h-Inshey rish jeih as daeed bleeaney. Ren eh boallaghyn, thieyn as droghadyn, as ren eh claghyn son y cheeill ayns y valley. Nish ta'n dreeym echey croym, as t'eh shooyl dy moal. Agh ta ny laueyn echey foast lajer.

Ta mac-y-vac echey, Tristram, shey bleeaney jeig d'eash. Un laa 'sy tourey, haink Tristram gys thie e shenn-ayr.

“Bare lhiam ve ny masoonagh, myr oo hene,” dooyrt eh.

Va Algernon goaill boggey. Va jerkallys echey rieau dy jinnagh fer jeh'n lught-thie echey yn obbyr shoh y ghoaill. Cha row y jerkallys shen echey son e vac hene, son ta'n mac echey ny ynseyder. Agh nish, va jerkallys noa echey.

“Nee shin leac son oaie dty shenn-shenn-voir,” dooyrt Algernon. “Cha row clagh mie erbee er yn oaie eck rieau.”

Ec y thie-obbree echey, va clagh vooar ghlass. She clagh hryal v'ayn.

“Ta clagh hryal feer chreoi,” dooyrt Algernon. “Ta'n tryal shoh veih'n twoaie jeh'n ellan. Bee eh tannaghtyn rish keead bleeaney.”

Ghow Algernon slatt veih'n voalley.

“Ren my ayr hene ymmyd jeh'n slatt shoh,” dooyrt eh. “She slatt cruinn ee. Towse yn chlagh lhiat.”

Ren Tristram towse yn leac lesh y slatt: v'ee un slatt er liurid, as lieh slatt er lheead. Eisht ren Algernon croymmey harrish y chlagh, as hug eh cowraghyn urree.

Rish shiaghtin, ren ad gobbraghey marish y cheilley. Ren Tristram giarrey yn ennym, as ren Algernon giarrey yn date. Va'n date ruggyr as yn date baase eck er y leac: 1901 as 1979.

“Ta mee er lhaih mychione ogham,” dooyrt Tristram. “Ta ogham er shenn claghyn ayns Ellan Vannin. Foddee shin yn ennym eck y screeu ayns ogham neesht?”

Va Algernon booiagh. “She smooinaght mie ee. Ren ny shenn masoonee ogham er claghyn son ny marroo. Nee shin eh myr shen.”

Myr shen, va'n ennym ayns lettyryn noa, as ayns ogham er oirr y leac.

Er y jerrey, haink ben veih'n valley gys y thie-obbree. Va'n sheshey eck er gheddyn baase. Ren Algernon loayrt rish y ven dy meein, as ren eh feysht jee mychione e sheshey. Hug eh traa jee.

Lurg da'n ven goll magh, dooyrt Algernon rish Tristram: “Ta ny laueyn lajer feme ec masoonagh, agh ta cooyrtoilid feme echey neesht. Ta sleih çheet hood ec y traa smessey jeh nyn mea. Ta cooyrtoilid ny smoo scanshoil na'n chlagh hene.”

Feyshtyn:
Quoi va ny masoonagh rish jeih as daeed bleeaney?
Va Algernon Teare ny masoonagh ayns Purt ny h-Inshey.
Cre'n jerkallys v'ec Algernon rieau?
Va jerkallys echey dy jinnagh fer jeh'n lught-thie echey yn obbyr y ghoaill.
Cre'n chlagh v'ayns y leac?
She clagh hryal v'ayn, veih'n twoaie jeh'n ellan.
Cre ren ad giarrey er oirr y leac?
Ren ad giarrey yn ennym ayns ogham.
Cre ta feme ec masoonagh, rere Algernon?
Ta laueyn lajer as cooyrtoilid feme echey.

lessons.title: Shiaghtin 'sy arragh ec y thie-ollee
lessons.summary: Twelve-year-old Imogen from Douglas spends a spring week on the farm of her grandmother Griselda Kinvig near Ramsey: they look at the old horse plough of Griselda's grandfather, sow corn, spread muck from the dunghill on a barren field, watch a flock of sheep, chase rabbits from the young corn, and find a toad under the rain barrel, while a robin follows them everywhere.
lessons.text:
Ta Imogen daa vlein jeig d'eash, as t'ee cummal ayns Doolish. 'Sy arragh, hie ee son shiaghtin gys thie-ollee e shenn-voir, Griselda Kinvig, faggys da Rhumsaa.

Er y chied voghrey, ghow Griselda ee gys y thie-shamyr. Va keeaght shenn ayn, jeant ass yiarn as fuygh.

“She keeaght my shenn-ayr ee shoh,” dooyrt Griselda. “Va cabbyl echey, as va'n cabbyl tayrn y cheeaght trooid y thalloo. Nish ta greieyn noa ain, agh ta mee freayll y cheeaght shenn son cooinaght.”

Lurg shen, hie ad magh gys y vagher. Va'n thalloo er ny hyndaa hannah, as hug ad yn arroo 'sy thalloo. Va spittag beg shassoo er y voalley, as v'ee jeeaghyn orroo.

“Ta'n spittag shoh geiyrt orrym dy chooilley arragh,” dooyrt Griselda. “T'ee shirrey beishteigyn 'sy thalloo noa.”

Ec y jerrey jeh'n vagher, va boayl ny ghaa gyn faiyr erbee. Va'n thalloo shen shiast.

“Cre'n fa ta'n thalloo shoh shiast?” dooyrt Imogen.

“Ta ram claghyn as geinnagh ayn,” dooyrt Griselda. “Cha nel bee dy liooar ayn son ny lossreeyn. Agh ta fys aym cre'n aght dy jannoo eh mie.”

Ghow ad Imogen gys y thorran faggys da thie ny bwoaillee. Va'n thorran mooar as ard, as va soar lajer echey. Ren Imogen cur yn eddin eck fo e laue.

“Ta'n thorran shoh lane dy vee son y thalloo,” dooyrt Griselda. Rish daa laa, ren ad cur y thorran er y thalloo shiast.

'Syn astyr, ren ad jeeaghyn er y chronk. Va shioltane mooar kirree er y chronk, as va kirree aegey 'sy shioltane. Va'n moddey cur y shioltane sheese gys y thie-ollee, as va'n spittag shassoo er y yiat, jeeaghyn er y shioltane.

Er y trass laa, va conning 'sy vagher arroo. Eisht haink conning elley, as fer elley.

“Ta ny conneeyn shen gee yn arroo aeg!” dooyrt Griselda. Roie Imogen nyn yei, as roie ny conneeyn ersooyl gys y clea.

Ec corneil thie ny bwoaillee, va stoandey mooar. Va'n stoandey shen freayll ushtey ny fliaghey son ny lossreeyn. Tra ren Imogen y stoandey y ghleashagh, va beayf fo.

“Ta beayf aym!” dooyrt Imogen. Va'n beayf doan as fliugh, agh cha row aggle er Imogen.

“Cur yn beayf fo'n stoandey reesht,” dooyrt Griselda. “T'eh gee ny shellooyn as ny beishteigyn. She carrey dooin eh.”

Er y laa jerree, cha row Imogen booiagh dy row ee goll thie.

“Tar reesht 'sy tourey,” dooyrt Griselda. “Bee'n arroo ard eisht, as bee shin fakin vel y thalloo shiast ny share.”

Feyshtyn:
Quoi v'ec y cheeaght shenn?
Va'n cheeaght ec shenn-ayr Griselda, as va cabbyl echey dy tayrn ee.
Cre'n fa va'n thalloo shiast?
Va ram claghyn as geinnagh ayn.
Cre ren ad lesh y thorran?
Ren ad cur y thorran er y thalloo shiast.
Cre va ny conneeyn jannoo 'sy vagher?
V'ad gee yn arroo aeg.
Cre va fo'n stoandey?
Va beayf fo'n stoandey.

lessons.title: Lettyr veih naunt ayns y Çhapaan
lessons.summary: In a letter to her niece Jessamy in Castletown, Perdita, who teaches English in Okinawa in the south of Japan, writes about learning Japanese, her lodging in the house of ninety-year-old Yaeko and Yaeko's great-granddaughter, high prices and spices in the food, the tourism of the islands, a coral reef with turtles, and the party Yaeko's family held for her birthday.
lessons.text:
Okinawa, 3 Mee Houney

Jessamy veen,

Hooar mee dty lettyr, as ta mee goaill boggey dy vel oo jannoo dy mie 'sy scoill. Ta dty naunt Perdita nish ayns Okinawa son tree meeghyn, as ta ram dy insh dhyt aym.

Ta mee gynsaghey Baarle ayns scoill aeg, as ta mee hene gynsaghey Shapaanish. Ta Shapaanish feer doillee! Ta tree aghtyn screeuee ayns Shapaanish, as ta ram lettyryn ayn. Agh ta ny paitçhyn 'sy scoill dooie dou, as ta mee abyl focklyn beggey ayns Shapaanish y loayrt nish.

Hooar mee aaght ayns thie ben ennagh enmyssit Yaeko. T'ee kiare feed as jeih bleeaney d'eash. Ta inneen-vac y vac eck cummal 'sy thie neesht. Ta'n aaght aym beg as glen, as cha nel y prios ard. Ayns thieyn oast, ta'n prios son aaght feer ard.

Ta prios y vee ard ayns Okinawa neesht, er-yn-oyr dy vel y chooid smoo jeh'n vee çheet veih'n Çhapaan mooar. Agh ta'n bee blastal. Ta Yaeko cur spios er y vee dy chooilley laa: spios buigh, spios jiarg as spios ghlass. Va'n spios jiarg ro heh dou hoshiaght, agh nish s'mie lhiam eh.

She turrysaght yn obbyr smoo ayns Okinawa. Ta sleih çheet veih'n Çhapaan as veih çheeraghyn elley son y ghrian as y traie. Ta turrysaght mie son ny shappyn, agh ta Yaeko gra dy vel turrysaght ro vooar nish, as dy vel y traie ro lane 'sy tourey.

Jedoonee shoh chaie, hie mee fo'n ushtey lesh carrey jeh'n scoill. Va creg corralagh aalin ayn, lane dy eeastyn beggey as daahghyn ooilley. As honnick mee turtyl! Va'n turtyl mooar as glass, as v'eh snaue dy meein harrish y chreg corralagh. Ta Yaeko gra dy row ny smoo turtylyn ayn tra v'ee aeg.

Ec y jerrey, va my laa ruggyr ayn Jesarn. Ren lught-thie Yaeko giense dou! Haink ny paitçhyn veih'n scoill gys y giense, as hug ad arrane ayns Shapaanish. Va bee blastal ec y giense, as hie ny shenn deiney as ny paitçhyn er daunsey marish y cheilley.

Ta mee smooinaghtyn ort dy mennick. Insh dty voir dy vel mee braew.

Lesh graih,
Dty naunt Perdita

Feyshtyn:
Quoi ta Perdita?
She naunt Jessamy ee: t'ee gynsaghey Baarle ayns Okinawa.
Raad hooar Perdita aaght?
Hooar ee aaght ayns thie Yaeko.
Cre'n fa ta prios y vee ard ayns Okinawa?
Er-yn-oyr dy vel y chooid smoo jeh'n vee çheet veih'n Çhapaan mooar.
Cre honnick Perdita fo'n ushtey?
Honnick ee creg corralagh as turtyl mooar glass.
Cre ren lught-thie Yaeko son laa ruggyr Perdita?
Ren ad giense jee.

lessons.title: Yn skaa as y maghouin
lessons.summary: On a winter evening Rowena reads her eight-year-old grandson Oswin an old tale in poetic prose from a book her own grandmother gave her: a poor young soldier, Ector, has no armour for the king's tournament, but a prophet tells him he will save the town; on the day of the tournament a terrible bear comes out of the forest, and Ector stops it with nothing but his old shield, so the people call him their saviour.
lessons.text:
Ayns y geurey, ta Oswin, ny mac-y-vac ec Rowena, cummal ec e thie rish shiaghtin. T'eh hoght bleeaney d'eash. Dy chooilley astyr, ta Rowena lhaih skeeal da ass shenn lioar.

“Hug my shenn-voir hene y lioar shoh dou,” dooyrt Rowena. “Ta'n skeeal screeuit ayns prose, cha nel ayns daanyn. Agh she prose bardoil t'ayn: ta ny focklyn aalin myr arrane.”

Eisht ren ee lhaih:

“Va dooinney aeg ayn keayrt dy row, as Ector va'n ennym echey. V'eh ny sidoor, agh v'eh boght. Va skaa echey, shenn skaa jeant ass fuygh, agh cha row eilley echey. Cha row ny sidooryn elley dooie da, son va eilley yiarn oc ooilley.

“Ren y ree fockley magh tournamint mooar. Haink sidooryn veih dy chooilley ard gys y tournamint, as v'ad ooilley ayns eilley ghial.

“Er y laa roish y tournamint, haink shenn dooinney gys Ector. She faaishnagh v'ayn. Dooyrt y faaishnagh: ‘Cha jean oo cosney ayns y tournamint, agh nee oo sauail y balley. As bee'n sleih genmys oo nyn saualtagh.’

“Cha row Ector toiggal. Kys oddagh sidoor boght gyn eilley ve ny saualtagh?

“Er laa yn tournamint, va'n sleih ooilley ec y vagher. Eisht haink sheean atçhimagh veih'n cheyll. Haink maghouin mooar magh, as v'eh roie noi'n sleih. Va'n maghouin doo as atçhimagh, as va aggle er ooilley. Roie ny sidooryn ayns nyn eilley ghial ersooyl.

“Agh hass Ector roish y maghouin, as cha row echey agh e shenn skaa. Ren y maghouin bwoailley y skaa reesht as reesht, agh cha ren Ector goll er y chooylloo. Ec y jerrey, va'n maghouin lag, as hie eh thie gys y cheyll.

“Eisht dooyrt y sleih: ‘She Ector nyn saualtagh!’ As va fockle y faaishnagh feer.”

Hug Rowena y lioar sheese.

“Va ny sidooryn elley ayns eilley,” dooyrt Oswin, “agh v'ad roie ersooyl. Cha row agh skaa ec Ector, as cha row eh roie.”

“Shen eh,” dooyrt Rowena. “Ta'n skeeal gra nagh vel yn eilley scanshoil, agh yn cree.”

“Vel faaishnagh erbee ayn nish?” dooyrt Oswin.

“Cha nel, my chree. Agh ta'n shenn lioar aym, as nee'm y lioar shoh y choyrt dhyt, tra vees oo mooar. Eisht foddee oo lhaih y prose bardoil shoh da dty phaitçhyn hene.”

Feyshtyn:
Quoi hug y lioar da Rowena?
Hug e shenn-voir hene y lioar jee.
Cre'n sorçh skeeal t'ayns y lioar?
She skeeal ayns prose bardoil t'ayn.
Cre v'ec Ector, as cre nagh row echey?
Va shenn skaa jeant ass fuygh echey, agh cha row eilley echey.
Cre dooyrt y faaishnagh rish Ector?
Dooyrt eh dy jinnagh Ector sauail y balley, as dy beagh y sleih genmys eh nyn saualtagh.
Cre haink magh ass y cheyll?
Haink maghouin mooar atçhimagh magh.
Cre ren Ector tra haink y maghouin?
Hass eh roish y maghouin lesh e shenn skaa, as cha ren eh roie.

lessons.title: Obbyr-scoill mychione y Ghaelg
lessons.summary: Fifteen-year-old Piers must write about Manx for school, and his grandmother Hildegard Moorhouse, a retired linguist, helps him: Manx speakers are a small minority; Manx has few cases, Latin six; she explains a theory of how cases are lost, the dependent form of the verb after cha and nagh, stress on the first syllable, sounds as discrete units, and the glottal stop of London English; his teacher's criticism of his first draft was that it was too short, but his new work is suitable for the school's journal.
lessons.text:
Ta Piers queig bleeaney jeig d'eash, as ta obbyr-scoill echey: t'eh screeu mychione y Ghaelg. Va'n chied screeuyn echey ro ghiare. Va cremeydys ec yn ynseyder: “Ta'n obbyr shoh ro ghiare, as cha nel fys dy liooar ayn mychione y ghrammeydys.”

Myr shen, hie Piers gys e shenn-voir, Hildegard Moorhouse. Va Hildegard ny çhengoayllee ec ollooscoill rish ymmodee bleeantyn.

“Cha nel y cremeydys shen olk,” dooyrt ee. “Foddee shin obbyr share y yannoo. Hoshiaght: quoi ta loayrt Gaelg?”

“Cha nel agh beggan sleih,” dooyrt Piers.

“She mynlught beg ad,” dooyrt Hildegard. “Ayns Ellan Vannin, ta'n mynlught ta loayrt Gaelg feer veg, agh t'eh gaase.”

Eisht ren ee loayrt mychione case.

“Ayns Ladjyn, ta shey case ayn. Ta case er lheh ayn son ‘jeh’, as case elley son ‘da’. Ta beggan caseyn ayns Gaelg nish, agh va ny smoo ayn keayrt dy row. Ta çhoarym ec çhengoayllee: tra ta ny sheeanyn ec jerrey ny focklyn goll er coayl, ta ny caseyn goll er coayl neesht. Cha nel shickyrys ayn dy vel y çhoarym shoh feer, agh she çhoarym mie t'ayn.”

“As ny breearyn?” dooyrt Piers.

“Ta cummey croghagh ec ny breearyn. Ta shin gra ‘ta mee’, agh ‘cha nel mee’ as ‘nagh vel mee’. She ‘vel’ yn cummey croghagh. T'eh croghagh er ‘cha’ ny ‘nagh’ roish.”

Eisht ren ad loayrt mychione stroos.

“'Sy Ghaelg, ta'n stroos er y chied ayrn jeh'n fockle dy mennick,” dooyrt Hildegard. “Ayns ‘balley’, ta'n stroos er y chied ayrn. Agh ayns focklyn ennagh, ta'n stroos er y nah ayrn.”

“Ta fys aym nish cre ta stroos,” dooyrt Piers.

“Nish, ny sheeanyn,” dooyrt ee. “Ta ny sheeanyn ayns çhengey myr unnidyn discreajagh. Ta'n chied sheean ayns ‘ta’ as y chied sheean ayns ‘da’ daa unnid discreajagh, son ta ‘ta’ as ‘da’ daa fockle er lheh.”

Ec y jerrey, dooyrt Hildegard mychione y sheean sluggidagh. “Ayns Baarle Lunnin, cha nel sleih gra yn chied sheean ayns ‘ta’ ayns mean focklyn ennagh: ta corockle sluggidagh ayns e ynnyd. T'eh jeant 'sy scoarnagh. Ta'n corockle sluggidagh ayns ymmodee çhengaghyn.”

Lurg shiaghtin, hug Piers yn obbyr noa da'n ynseyder. Cha row cremeydys erbee ec yn ynseyder nish.

“Ta'n obbyr shoh freggyragh son lioar ny scoill,” dooyrt ee. “Nee shin eh y chur 'sy lioar.”

Feyshtyn:
Cre va'n cremeydys ec yn ynseyder?
Dooyrt ee dy row yn obbyr ro ghiare.
Quoi ta loayrt Gaelg ayns Ellan Vannin?
Mynlught beg ta loayrt Gaelg, agh t'eh gaase.
Vel ram caseyn ayns Ladjyn?
Ta. Ta shey case ayns Ladjyn.
Cre'n cummey croghagh jeh ‘ta’?
She ‘vel’ yn cummey croghagh.
Cre dooyrt yn ynseyder mychione yn obbyr noa?
Dooyrt ee dy row yn obbyr freggyragh son lioar ny scoill.
Cre ta jeant 'sy scoarnagh?
Ta'n corockle sluggidagh jeant 'sy scoarnagh.

lessons.title: Fo'n mynreayrtan
lessons.summary: Sylvester Hatherley, a retired biology teacher, takes his ten-year-old granddaughter Primrose to a wooded glen and they bring home a thistle leaf, a caterpillar, a spider, a butterfly's wing and a stone; under his old microscope they see the little hairs on the prickly leaf, the green plastids in its cells, the scaly wing, and the spider, an arthropod; the caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly and a leaf feeder, the worms in the soil are beneficial, and the stone is inorganic.
lessons.text:
Va Sylvester Hatherley ny ynseyder bea-oaylleeaght rish ymmodee bleeantyn. Nish t'eh shenn, agh ta mynreayrtan foast echey 'sy thie. Ta e inneen-vac, Primrose, jeih bleeaney d'eash, as s'mie lhee ooilley ny reddyn bio.

Un Jesarn, ghow Sylvester Primrose gys glion keylljagh faggys da'n thie. Va'n glion lane dy viljyn: va'n raad keylljagh, as va'n soilshey glass fo ny biljyn.

Ren ad çhaglym reddyn son y mynreayrtan: duillag veih onnane, praddag, sniengan beg, skian foillycan va er y thalloo, as clagh.

“Ta'n duillag shoh friogganagh!” dooyrt Primrose.

“Ta, ta'n onnane friogganagh,” dooyrt Sylvester. “Ta'n lus coadey eh hene myr shen.”

Ec y thie, ren ad cur y duillag fo'n mynreayrtan. Va renaigyn beggey er y duillag, myr folt. Va dagh renaig feer veg as geyre.

“Ta renaigyn er ny duillagyn ec ymmodee lossreeyn,” dooyrt Sylvester. “Ta ny renaigyn freayll yn ushtey 'sy duillag.”

Eisht ren ad jeeaghyn ny smoo mooadaghey. Va killagyn ayn, as ayns ny killagyn, va reddyn beggey glassey.

“She plastaidyn ad shen,” dooyrt Sylvester. “Ta'n plastaid glass jannoo bee son y lus veih soilshey ny greiney. Gyn ny plastaidyn, cha bee lus erbee bio.”

Lurg shen, ren ad jeeaghyn er y phraddag.

“Ta'n phraddag shoh ny laarvey,” dooyrt Sylvester. “Ayns tammylt, bee'n laarvey er ny hyndaa ayns foillycan. As she beeagheyder er duillagyn y laarvey. T'ee gee duillagyn veih moghrey gys oie.”

“As ta beeagheyder elley ayns y garey: yn sniengan,” dooyrt Primrose. “T'eh gee beishteigyn.”

“Shen eh. As she arthropod yn sniengan. Ta crackan creoi er arthropod, as cassyn ayns ayrnyn. Ta'n phraddag ny arthropod neesht.”

Va skian y foillycan aalin fo'n mynreayrtan. V'ee scaaillagh: va ymmodee crottylyn beggey er, myr er eeast.

“Ta'n skian scaaillagh!” dooyrt Primrose. “Cha row fys aym er shen.”

“As ny beishteigyn 'sy thalloo,” dooyrt Sylvester. “T'ad foayssagh dooin. T'ad jannoo yn thalloo mie son ny lossreeyn. Cha nel ooilley ny beishteigyn foayssagh, agh ta ram jeu foayssagh.”

Ec y jerrey, hug Primrose y clagh fo'n mynreayrtan.

“Cha nel killagyn ayn,” dooyrt ee.

“Cha nel,” dooyrt Sylvester. “Cha row y chlagh bio rieau. She red neuorgaanagh t'ayn. Ta'n thalloo jeant ass reddyn orgaanagh as reddyn neuorgaanagh.”

Feyshtyn:
Raad hie Sylvester as Primrose?
Hie ad gys glion keylljagh faggys da'n thie.
Cre'n fa ta duillag yn onnane friogganagh?
Ta'n lus coadey eh hene myr shen.
Cre va er duillag yn onnane?
Va renaigyn beggey er, myr folt.
Cre ta ny plastaidyn jannoo?
Ta'n plastaid glass jannoo bee son y lus veih soilshey ny greiney.
Cre va er skian y foillycan?
Va'n skian scaaillagh: va ymmodee crottylyn beggey er.
Cre'n fa ta'n phraddag ny beeagheyder?
Son t'ee gee duillagyn veih moghrey gys oie.
Cre'n fa nagh row killagyn 'sy chlagh?
Er-yn-oyr nagh row y chlagh bio rieau: she red neuorgaanagh t'ayn.

lessons.title: Kiaull groamid son y shenn-ayr
lessons.summary: Bertram Skillicorn, eighty-six, has begun to forget names and days, and his granddaughter Odette, seventeen, is sad when she visits him on Sundays; the flowers on his window wither, and his old guitar case still smells of the tobacco he smoked for fifty years; Odette encourages him to play, and he remembers every blues song from his leisure hours when he was young: his face reddens, his eyes are bright, and she stops being sad.
lessons.text:
Ta Bertram Skillicorn shey bleeaney as kiare feed d'eash. Rish blein ny ghaa, t'eh jarrood reddyn. T'eh jarrood enmyn, as t'eh jarrood cre'n laa t'ayn. Keayrtyn t'eh jarrood dy vel e ven er gheddyn baase.

Dy chooilley Jedoonee, ta e inneen-vac, Odette, çheet gys e hie. T'ee shiaght bleeaney jeig d'eash. Ta Odette trimshagh tra t'ee fakin e shenn-ayr myr shoh. V'eh ny ghooinney lajer as tappee keayrt dy row.

Er Jedoonee ennagh, va ny blaaghyn er uinnag Bertram fioghey. Va ny duillagyn buigh, as va ny blaaghyn fioghey sheese.

“Ta ny blaaghyn shoh fioghey, Shenn-ayr,” dooyrt Odette. “Hig mee lesh blaaghyn noa.”

“Quoi uss?” dooyrt Bertram. Eisht dooyrt eh: “Odette! Myr shen. Cha jarrood mee dty ennym reesht.”

Va Odette trimshagh. Hie ee gys y chabbal dy gheddyn ushtey son ny blaaghyn, as hooar ee kishtey shenn. She kishtey gitar v'ayn. Tra ren ee y kishtey y osley, va soar tombagey ayn.

Ren Bertram tombagey y cheau rish jeih as daeed bleeaney. Ren eh scuirr jeih bleeaney er dy henney, agh va soar y tombagey foast 'sy kishtey.

“She yn gitar ayd ee shoh?” dooyrt Odette.

“She,” dooyrt Bertram. “Tra va mee aeg, va mee cloie y gitar ayns my lheiltys. Va mee gobbraghey ayns y phurt 'sy laa, as 'sy lheiltys aym, va mee cloie kiaull groamid.”

“Kiaull groamid?”

“She. Ta kiaull groamid trimshagh, agh t'eh aalin. Haink kiaull groamid veih America. Ta groamid ayns ny arraneyn, agh ta bea ayn neesht.”

Ren Odette greesaghey e shenn-ayr. “Cloie arrane dou, Shenn-ayr!”

“Cha nel fys aym nish,” dooyrt eh. Agh ren Odette greesaghey eh reesht, as ghow eh y gitar.

Eisht haink yindys. Ren Bertram cloie arrane groamid, as eisht fer elley, as fer elley. Cha ren eh jarrood un fockle, ny un sheean. Ren yn eddin echey jiargaghey, as va ny sooillyn echey soilsheanagh. Va ny sooillyn soilsheanagh myr sooillyn dooinney aeg.

Ren eddin Odette jiargaghey neesht, son v'ee goaill boggey. Cha row ee trimshagh nish.

“T'ou er jarrood ennym y laa,” dooyrt ee, “agh cha nel oo er jarrood y kiaull.”

“Cha jarrood mee y kiaull dy bragh,” dooyrt Bertram.

Feyshtyn:
Cre ta Bertram jarrood?
T'eh jarrood enmyn, as cre'n laa t'ayn.
Cre va ny blaaghyn er yn uinnag jannoo?
Va ny blaaghyn fioghey.
Cre va 'sy chishtey gitar?
Va soar tombagey 'sy chishtey.
Cre va Bertram jannoo ayns e lheiltys tra v'eh aeg?
V'eh cloie kiaull groamid er y gitar.
Cre ren Odette tra dooyrt Bertram nagh row fys echey?
Ren ee greesaghey eh reesht.
Kys va Bertram jeeaghyn tra v'eh cloie?
Ren yn eddin echey jiargaghey, as va ny sooillyn echey soilsheanagh.

lessons.title: Yn ven-etlee 'sy lught-thie
lessons.summary: Thirteen-year-old Lettice, who likes to draw, looks through an old box with her grandmother Augusta and finds papers about her great-grandmother Evangeline Pennyfeather, who in 1936 flew a small aeroplane of wood and cloth from Douglas to the western coast of Ireland: aviation was an innovation then, the newspapers gave her great publicity, an illustrator drew her plane, her engine gave off black smoke over the sea, she won status as a woman in a man's world, and she wrote that in the sky she forgot earthly worries.
lessons.text:
Ta Lettice tree bleeaney jeig d'eash, as s'mie lhee tayrn. Un astyr, ren ee as e shenn-voir, Augusta, kishtey shenn y osley 'sy thie eck.

“Ta ny pabyryn shoh mychione my voir,” dooyrt Augusta. “Va my voir, Evangeline Pennyfeather, ny ben-etlee.”

Va ram pabyryn as jallooyn 'sy kishtey. Ayns jalloo ennagh, va ben aeg shassoo roish etlan beg.

“Ayns 1936, ren y voir aym etlagh veih Doolish gys oirr eearagh Nerin,” dooyrt Augusta. “Ec y traa shen, va etlanys feer noa. She noaid mooar v'ayn, as va sleih goaill yindys jeh'n noaid shen. Cha row agh beggan sleih er etlagh rieau, as cha row agh beggan mraane ayns etlanys.”

Va'n etlan jeant ass fuygh as eaddagh. She stoo covestagh v'ayn: va fuygh, eaddagh as yiarn 'sy stoo covestagh cheddin.

“Va'n etlan feer eddrym,” dooyrt Augusta. “Va stoo covestagh myr shen eddrym, agh cha row eh lajer.”

Ghow Lettice pabyr-naight shenn ass y kishtey. Va soilsheydys mooar ayns ny pabyryn-naight son Evangeline. Va'n ennym eck er y chied ayrn jeh dagh pabyr.

“Va soilsheydys myr shen noa da ben aeg,” dooyrt Augusta. “Va'n soilsheydys mie son etlanys, agh cha row eh aashagh jee.”

Ayns pabyr-naight elley, va jalloo tayrnit jeh'n etlan. Va tayrneyder er jannoo yn jalloo.

“Quoi yn tayrneyder?” dooyrt Lettice.

“Cha nel fys aym,” dooyrt Augusta. “Agh she tayrneyder mie v'ayn. Jeeagh: ta'n jaagh doo ayns y jalloo.”

Va lioar-laa Evangeline 'sy kishtey neesht. Ren Augusta lhaih ass:

“‘Harrish y vooir, ren y greie jaagh doo y vrooightey. V'eh brooightey jaagh rish lieh oor, as va aggle orrym. Agh haink mee gys y thalloo eearagh, as ren mee çheet sheese er magher ec y traie.’”

“As cre haink er y keimeeaght eck?” dooyrt Lettice.

“Ec y traa shen, cha row keimeeaght ard ec mraane,” dooyrt Augusta. “Agh lurg yn etlagh shen, va keimeeaght vooar eck. Va sleih ooashlaghey ee.”

Ec y jerrey, ren Augusta lhaih un red elley ass y lioar-laa:

“‘'Sy speyr, ta mee jarrood ooilley ny reddyn seihlltagh: argid, obbyr as boirey. Cha nel agh yn aer as y ghrian ayn.’”

“Ta mee goaill toiggal jee,” dooyrt Lettice. “Tra ta mee tayrn, ta mee jarrood ny reddyn seihlltagh neesht.”

Eisht ghow Lettice pabyr, as ren ee jalloo jeh'n etlan beg. Bare lhee ve ny tayrneyder, myr y tayrneyder va tayrn etlan Evangeline.

Feyshtyn:
Cre'n fa va etlanys ny noaid ayns 1936?
Va etlanys feer noa, as cha row agh beggan sleih er etlagh rieau.
Raad ren Evangeline etlagh ayns 1936?
Ren ee etlagh veih Doolish gys oirr eearagh Nerin.
Cre'n stoo v'ayns yn etlan?
Va stoo covestagh ayn, jeant ass fuygh, eaddagh as yiarn.
Cre va'n greie brooightey harrish y vooir?
V'eh brooightey jaagh doo.
Cre haink er keimeeaght Evangeline lurg yn etlagh?
Va keimeeaght vooar eck, as va sleih ooashlaghey ee.
Cre ta Lettice jarrood tra t'ee tayrn?
T'ee jarrood ny reddyn seihlltagh.

lessons.title: Kishtey pabyryn y shenn-ayr
lessons.summary: Sixteen-year-old Ivo helps his grandfather Zachariah Fitzroy, eighty-eight, sort a box of old papers: Zachariah grew up in poverty in Douglas, became a socialist, and in 1962 went to a workers' congress in Berlin, from which he kept a few German marks; he believed in common ownership of land and factories and saw his family's opposition as only an obstacle; Ivo does not agree with everything, but they agree that a house and food are necessary for everyone, and that the common people must have a voice.
lessons.text:
Ta Ivo shey bleeaney jeig d'eash. Un Jesarn, hie eh gys thie e shenn-ayr, Zachariah Fitzroy, dy chur oardagh er kishtey shenn dy phabyryn. Ta Zachariah hoght bleeaney as kiare feed d'eash.

“Ta my vea ooilley 'sy kishtey shoh,” dooyrt Zachariah.

Va jalloo shenn 'sy kishtey: thie beg ayns Doolish, as shiaght paitçhyn roish y dorrys.

“Va mee ruggit 'sy thie shen,” dooyrt Zachariah. “Va boghtinys mooar ayn. Va my ayr gobbraghey 'sy phurt, agh cha row argid dy liooar ain. Va boghtinys ec dagh lught-thie 'sy straid. Tra va mee aeg, va mee smooinaghtyn: cre'n fa ta boghtinys ec ny sleih cadjinagh, as argid ec beggan sleih?”

“As shen-y-fa haink oo dy ve ny soshiallagh?” dooyrt Ivo.

“Shen eh. Hooar mee soshiallys ayns lioar ec y lioarlann. Ta soshiallys gra dy lhisagh shellooderaght y thallooin as ny thieyn-obbree ve ec ny sleih cadjinagh, cha nel ec beggan sleih berçhagh.”

Ghow Ivo pabyr elley ass y kishtey. Va fockle ‘Cohaglym’ er.

“Ayns 1962, hie mee gys cohaglym 'sy Ghermaan, ayns Berlin,” dooyrt Zachariah. “Va obbreeyn veih ymmodee çheeraghyn ec y cohaglym. Va shin loayrt mychione soshiallys, mychione shellooderaght as mychione boghtinys.”

Fo ny pabyryn, va argid shenn: tree margyn.

“Margyn ass y Ghermaan,” dooyrt Zachariah. “Cha row agh beggan margyn aym. Va mee ceau ny margyn elley er bee.”

“Va dty lught-thie booiagh lesh y soshiallys ayd?” dooyrt Ivo.

“Cha row,” dooyrt Zachariah. “Va my ayr hene noi. Va shen ny bac. Va bac elley ayn neesht: cha row argid aym son ollooscoill. Agh cha ren ny bac shen m'obbyr y lhiettal.”

Ren Ivo smooinaghtyn son tammylt. “Cha nel mee credjal ayns dy chooilley red t'ou gra,” dooyrt eh. “Cha nel mee shickyr dy lhisagh shellooderaght dy chooilley hie-obbree ve ec y reiltys.”

“Shen dty varel,” dooyrt Zachariah. “Ta shen mie. Agh ta red ennagh ymmyrçhagh, nagh vel?”

“Ta,” dooyrt Ivo. “Ta thie ymmyrçhagh da dy chooilley pheiagh. As ta bee ymmyrçhagh. As ta coraa ymmyrçhagh ec ny sleih cadjinagh.”

Va Zachariah booiagh. “She soshiallagh beg oo, ga nagh vel oo credjal eh!”

Hug eh un marg da Ivo. “Freill shoh,” dooyrt eh. “Son cooinaght.”

Feyshtyn:
Cre'n aght va bea Zachariah tra v'eh aeg?
Va boghtinys mooar ayn, as cha row argid dy liooar ec y lught-thie.
Raad hooar Zachariah soshiallys?
Hooar eh soshiallys ayns lioar ec y lioarlann.
Raad hie Zachariah ayns 1962?
Hie eh gys cohaglym 'sy Ghermaan, ayns Berlin.
Cre va'n bac v'ec Zachariah?
Va e ayr hene noi, as cha row argid echey son ollooscoill.
Cre ta ymmyrçhagh da dy chooilley pheiagh, rere Ivo?
Ta thie as bee ymmyrçhagh, as coraa son ny sleih cadjinagh.
Cre hug Zachariah da Ivo?
Hug eh un marg da.

lessons.title: Yn mwyllin er yn awin
lessons.summary: Nigella, an archaeologist of sixty-five, takes her eleven-year-old grandson Wystan to the old mill where her grandfather worked: the river drains into the sea below, a sluice let water into the side channel for the wheel, the walls are wet with damp, and in a cold room the family cooled the milk in water from the stream; behind the mill she digs in the old rubbish heap, as archaeologists do, and Wystan finds a piece of a wax candle that his great-great-grandfather may have used.
lessons.text:
Ta Nigella queig bleeaney as tree feed d'eash, as t'ee ny shenndaalee. Rish ymmodee bleeantyn, t'ee er ve ronsaghey shenn reddyn 'sy thalloo. Un laa 'sy tourey, ghow ee e mac-y-vac, Wystan, gys shenn vwyllin 'sy glion. T'eh nane jeig d'eash.

“Va my shenn-ayr gobbraghey ayns y vwyllin shoh,” dooyrt Nigella. “Va'n lught-thie ain cummal ayn rish keead bleeaney.”

Va'n mwyllin faggys da awin. Ta'n awin shen roie sheese trooid y glion, as ta'n awin teaumey stiagh 'sy vooir faggys da'n traie.

“Raad ta'n ushtey goll?” dooyrt Wystan.

“Ta'n awin teaumey 'sy vooir,” dooyrt Nigella. “Agh roish shen, va'n ushtey goll trooid y vwyllin. Jeeagh: shoh yn cooylley.”

Va cooylley shenn yiarn ayns y voalley clagh. Va'n cooylley shen lhiggey yn ushtey stiagh ayns strooan çheualagh.

“Tra va my shenn-ayr fosley yn cooylley, va'n ushtey roie trooid y strooan çheualagh gys y queeyl,” dooyrt Nigella. “As va'n queeyl çhyndaa. Tra va'n cooylley dooint, va'n ushtey tannaghtyn 'syn awin.”

Hie ad stiagh 'sy vwyllin. Va'n aer feayr, as va fliughid er ny boallaghyn.

“Ta fliughid er dy chooilley voalley,” dooyrt Wystan.

“Ta,” dooyrt Nigella. “Ta'n awin ro faggys. Ta fliughid mooar ayns shenn thieyn faggys da ushtey.”

Ayns shamyr veg, va claghyn mooarey er y laare, as va strooan beg roie fo. “Shoh raad va'n lught-thie feayraghey yn vainney,” dooyrt Nigella. “Va'n ushtey feer feayr, as v'eh feayraghey yn vainney son yn oie. Cha row greie ayn son feayraghey ec y traa shen.”

Eisht hie ad gys cooyl y vwyllin. Va thalloo ard ayn, as va faiyr er.

“Shoh yn smooirlagh,” dooyrt Nigella. “Va'n lught-thie ceau ooilley yn smooirlagh oc ayns shoh. Ta shenndaaleeyn goaill boggey jeh smooirlagh, son ta shennaghys ayn.”

Ren ad ronsaghey 'sy smooirlagh. Hooar ad peeshyn dy ghlonney brisht, as clagh beg. Eisht hooar Wystan red beg buigh.

“Cre shoh?”

“She peesh dy chainle kereagh,” dooyrt Nigella. “Ec y traa shen, va cainle kereagh ny red mie, son v'ee soilshaghey dy mie. Foddee dy row y chainle shoh ec dty shenn-shenn-ayr.”

Ren Wystan yn chainle kereagh y ghoaill thie lesh. “Bee mish ny shenndaalee neesht, tra vees mee mooar,” dooyrt eh.

Feyshtyn:
Raad ta'n awin teaumey?
Ta'n awin teaumey stiagh 'sy vooir faggys da'n traie.
Cre va'n cooylley jannoo?
V'eh lhiggey yn ushtey stiagh ayns y strooan çheualagh gys y queeyl.
Cre'n fa ta fliughid er ny boallaghyn?
Er-yn-oyr dy vel yn awin ro faggys.
Kys va'n lught-thie feayraghey yn vainney?
V'ad feayraghey eh ayns ushtey feer feayr veih strooan beg.
Cre hooar Wystan 'sy smooirlagh?
Hooar eh peesh dy chainle kereagh.
